hero_headline: Oracle EBS to Oracle Cloud Data Migration
hero_subheadline: Move from Oracle EBS to Oracle Cloud ERP (Fusion) with AI-powered data migration. Mine handles the FBDI template mapping, DFF conversion, and flexfield restructuring that make Oracle-to-Oracle Cloud migrations surprisingly complex.
overview_paragraphs: Oracle EBS to Oracle Cloud (Fusion) is Oracle's primary upgrade path and one of the largest enterprise migration programs happening today. With Oracle incentivizing Cloud ERP adoption through pricing pressure and new feature exclusivity, EBS customers face a clear mandate: migrate to the cloud or stay on increasingly expensive sustaining support. Despite being the same vendor, this is not a simple upgrade — Oracle Cloud uses a fundamentally different architecture with predefined business processes, limited customization, and a SaaS delivery model.

The technical challenge is paradoxically high for an intra-vendor migration. Oracle Cloud uses File-Based Data Import (FBDI) templates as the primary data loading mechanism — pre-formatted CSV files that must conform to exact column structures. EBS's deeply customized tables, Descriptive Flexfields (DFFs), Key Flexfields (KFFs), and lookup values must be mapped to Cloud's more standardized fields. The chart of accounts structure changes significantly — Cloud uses a tree-based segment hierarchy instead of EBS's value sets. Setup data (payment terms, tax codes, units of measure) must be recreated in Cloud before transaction data can load.

Oracle offers the Cloud Migration Toolkit, but it covers only a subset of data objects and assumes a relatively vanilla EBS installation. Companies with extensive customizations — which is most enterprise EBS deployments — face significant manual effort mapping DFFs, custom tables, and modified workflows to Cloud equivalents.

challenges.title: FBDI template formatting and sequencing
challenges.description: Oracle Cloud requires data to be loaded through FBDI (File-Based Data Import) templates — specific CSV formats with exact column ordering, mandatory fields, and lookup validations. Each business object (suppliers, customers, invoices, journals) has its own FBDI template with different rules. Generating correctly formatted FBDI files from EBS data requires precise transformation logic and loading sequences that respect cross-object dependencies.

challenges.title: Descriptive Flexfield (DFF) and global segment conversion
challenges.description: EBS DFFs use context-sensitive segments (ATTRIBUTE1–ATTRIBUTE15) whose meaning varies by context value. Oracle Cloud has its own DFF framework with different context structures and naming. Each EBS DFF context-segment combination must be mapped to the equivalent Cloud DFF or replaced with a Cloud extensible flexfield — and the data values converted accordingly.

challenges.title: Chart of accounts restructuring for Cloud segments
challenges.description: EBS uses accounting flexfield value sets with independent or dependent validation. Oracle Cloud uses tree-based hierarchies for each COA segment. The value set-to-tree conversion is non-trivial — parent-child relationships must be explicitly defined in Cloud's tree structure, and cross-validation rules must be recreated as Cloud segment rules.

challenges.title: Setup data migration before transaction data
challenges.description: Oracle Cloud requires all reference data (payment terms, tax codes, currencies, UOM, supplier sites, customer sites) to be loaded and validated before any transaction data can import. The sequencing is strict — a single missing setup record causes entire FBDI loads to fail. Identifying the complete setup data dependency tree from EBS is a project in itself.

hero_headline: Sage Intacct to NetSuite Data Migration
hero_subheadline: Move from Sage Intacct to NetSuite with AI-powered data migration. Mine handles the dimensional accounting restructuring, custom object mapping, and multi-entity consolidation that make this migration deceptively complex.
overview_paragraphs: Sage Intacct to NetSuite migrations happen when companies outgrow Intacct's capabilities — typically triggered by the need for deeper inventory management, manufacturing, CRM integration, or multi-subsidiary consolidation beyond what Intacct provides natively. This is also common in M&A scenarios where the acquiring company runs NetSuite and needs to consolidate the acquired entity off Intacct. Despite both being cloud-native, the migration is more complex than most teams expect.

The core technical challenge is that Sage Intacct and NetSuite handle dimensional accounting differently. Intacct uses user-defined dimensions (UDDs) with up to 10 custom dimensions that can be applied at both transaction header and line level. NetSuite uses a fixed set of classification fields — subsidiary, department, class, and location — plus custom segments. Mapping Intacct's flexible dimensions to NetSuite's structured model requires careful analysis of how each dimension is actually used in reporting. Additionally, Intacct's contract billing and revenue recognition module has a different data model than NetSuite's Advanced Revenue Management.

Companies typically use CSV exports from Intacct combined with NetSuite's CSV import, but the dimensional restructuring and custom object translation require extensive manual transformation in spreadsheets before the data can load.

challenges.title: User-defined dimension mapping to NetSuite classifications
challenges.description: Sage Intacct supports up to 10 user-defined dimensions that can be freely applied to transactions. NetSuite uses a fixed structure — subsidiary, department, class, location — plus custom segments for additional dimensions. Not all Intacct dimensions map cleanly to NetSuite's classification fields. Some may need to become custom segments, custom fields, or even separate custom records in NetSuite.

challenges.title: Multi-entity consolidation differences
challenges.description: Intacct's multi-entity structure supports top-level and child entities with intercompany elimination rules. NetSuite's OneWorld uses a different subsidiary hierarchy and elimination subsidiary model. The consolidation structure, intercompany journal rules, and currency translation methods all need to be redesigned.

challenges.title: Contract billing and revenue recognition
challenges.description: Intacct's contract and revenue management module stores contract schedules, revenue recognition plans, and billing schedules in a purpose-built data model. NetSuite's Advanced Revenue Management uses different recognition methods and scheduling logic. Migrating active contracts with in-progress revenue schedules requires careful period-by-period reconciliation.

challenges.description: Intacct's Platform Services allow custom objects, custom transactions, and smart events. These have no direct NetSuite equivalent — each custom object must be analyzed and rebuilt as a NetSuite custom record with SuiteScript triggers replacing Intacct smart events.

hero_headline: Legacy Database to Salesforce Data Migration
hero_subheadline: Migrating from a custom database, Access, FoxPro, or homegrown system to Salesforce? Mine profiles any relational schema and automates the field mapping, data transformation, and validation — even when there's no documentation.
overview_paragraphs: Legacy database to Salesforce migrations are among the most varied and unpredictable migration types. The source could be anything — a Microsoft Access database that's been running for 15 years, a custom SQL Server or MySQL application, a FoxPro system, a FileMaker database, or even flat files exported from a decommissioned mainframe. These migrations are triggered when companies finally replace homegrown or legacy CRM systems with Salesforce, often as part of a broader digital transformation or after an acquisition where the acquired company has no standard CRM.

The core technical challenge is that legacy databases have no standard schema. Unlike migrating from SAP or Oracle where the table structures are known, a custom database requires discovery from scratch — table relationships must be inferred from foreign keys (if they exist), data types are often inconsistent, business logic lives in application code rather than the database, and there's rarely documentation. Field naming conventions are unpredictable, and the same conceptual entity (a customer) might be spread across multiple tables with no obvious join path.

Companies typically handle these migrations with brute-force manual effort — a database developer exports tables to CSV, a Salesforce admin manually maps columns to Salesforce fields, and someone spends weeks fixing data quality issues one field at a time. For large legacy databases with 50–200 tables, this process takes 4–8 months.

challenges.title: Undocumented schema discovery
challenges.description: Legacy databases rarely have ERD documentation or data dictionaries. Table and column names may be cryptic (TBL_CUST, FLD_01, STATUS_CD), relationships may not be enforced with foreign keys, and the same data may exist in multiple tables with no clear master. Mine's schema profiler infers relationships from data patterns — matching column values across tables to discover implicit joins.

challenges.title: Inconsistent data types and encoding
challenges.description: Legacy databases often store dates as strings, phone numbers as integers, booleans as Y/N or 1/0 or T/F, and currencies without decimal precision. Character encoding may vary between tables (Latin-1, Windows-1252, UTF-8). Every field needs content analysis, not just schema analysis, to determine the correct Salesforce target type.

challenges.title: No standard object model
challenges.description: Unlike ERP or CRM source systems that have standard concepts (customers, orders, invoices), legacy databases have bespoke object models. A 'Customers' table might combine what Salesforce separates into Accounts, Contacts, and Leads. A 'Transactions' table might contain sales orders, invoices, and payments mixed together with a type column. Decomposing these composite structures into Salesforce's object model requires business logic decisions.

challenges.title: Data quality issues accumulated over decades
challenges.description: Legacy databases accumulate data quality issues over their lifetime — duplicate records created by different application versions, orphaned foreign keys from deleted records, truncated fields from past schema changes, and test data mixed with production data. These issues aren't just migration problems — they need to be resolved before data enters Salesforce.
